problems: The new lookups materially strengthen locus-level ChIP support for ESR1 (H1), ZNF143 (H2), and FOXA1 (H4) in MCF-7: the reported ReMap peaks contain the variant. Their cell-type claims should no longer say that the evidence does not demonstrate binding at the variant locus. These peaks do not establish allele-specific occupancy or prove direct base-specific contact.

The H1 cell-type wording gives a 40 bp summit distance from E13, whereas E25 reports a nearest MCF-7 ReMap summit 28 bp away; H2 and H4 also have new peak-containing-variant evidence in E26 and E27, respectively.

For all chains, the target-gene assignment to TOX3 remains a proximity-based candidate, not a demonstrated regulatory effect. The variant does not overlap the nearby cCRE, and the evidence gives no direct cCRE-gene link or significant GTEx eQTL.
All binding-direction claims remain based on in-vitro family-screen predictions. The new ChIP evidence does not show that A has greater occupancy than G or establish a transcriptional direction.

No cited evidence establishes a breast-cancer association or a causal phenotype effect for this specific variant. The literature quotes do not provide a demonstrated link between this masked variant and the proposed chains.

A is better supported because ESR1 has ReMap peaks containing the variant across 139 MCF-7 peaks, with the nearest summit 28 bp away; B has only one ZNF143 MCF-7 peak containing the variant. ESR1’s mapped family model also predicts a stronger alt-binding effect than the ZNF143 model. Neither chain establishes a regulatory effect on TOX3 or a causal link to breast cancer.

Both chains have alt-favoring in-vitro binding predictions and nearby MCF7 ChIP evidence. ESR1 is better supported: it is more highly expressed in MCF7, its mapped family model predicts a larger alt-binding effect, and ReMap reports many ESR1 peaks containing the variant in MCF7. ZNF143 has a closer summit, but only one reported MCF7 peak containing the variant and a smaller predicted binding effect. The element, target-gene, and phenotype evidence does not distinguish the chains.

We found that CT (Cytocine-Thymine) and TT (Thymine -Thymine) genotypes, and T alleles of TOX3 rs[masked], were associated with BC risk (p = 0.034, p = 0.011, respectively).
SNP TOX3 rs[masked] was associated with positive progesterone receptors (PR) and triple-negative BC (TNBC) but not with estrogen receptor (ER) or HER2 reactivity.
TOX3 has been reported to be highly expressed in breast tumors and is closely related to estrogen receptors.
These findings suggest that TOX3 may play a vital role in the pathogenesis of breast cancer.
Differences in panel performance influenced association signals, including breast cancer candidate loci such as FGFR2, TOX3, and ESR1.

We curated a panel of 15 breast cancer associated genes ( BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PTEN, CHEK2, ATM, CDH1, PALB2, LSP1, MAP3K1, NF1, RECQL, TOX3, FANCD2, RAD51C ) based on clinical and epidemiological relevance.

Moderate-risk genes ( PALB2, RAD51C, CHEK2 ) showed intermediate levels of pathogenicity, while low-risk genes such as RECQL, TOX3 , and FANCD2 were predominantly enriched for variants of uncertain significance.

Key examples include promoter mutations [e.g., rs[masked] (Mouse double minute 2 homolog gene; MDM2)], enhancer mutations [e.g., rs[masked] (thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box family member 3 gene; TOX3)], and lncRNAs [e.g., HOX transcript antisense intergenic RNA (HOTAIR)] linked to progression, metastasis, and poor survival.
TFF1, FOXA1, ESR1, AGR2, TFF3, AGR3, GATA3, XBP1, SPDEF, and TOX3 were selected as hub genes by the MCC method, which were all upregulated.
